Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \\url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.'}]

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model to a smaller, more efficient "student" model. The primary objective is to create lightweight models that maintain high performance while reducing computational and memory requirements, which is crucial for deployment in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. The process typically involves training the student model to mimic the behavior of the teacher, often by learning from its rich output probability distributions or intermediate feature representations. This versatile framework has been successfully applied across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, and has been extended to address challenges in areas such as data privacy and domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, especially in natural language processing and computer vision, have become increasingly large and computationally expensive, hindering their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a key model compression technique to address this challenge. It operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient "student" model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. By transferring the rich knowledge from the teacher, the student can achieve comparable accuracy with a significantly smaller footprint. The applications of this framework extend beyond simple compression, including enhancing model performance, enabling domain adaptation, and facilitating learning in privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Deep Learning Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression paradigm where a compact 'student' model learns from a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This technique aims to create smaller, more efficient networks that retain the high performance of their cumbersome counterparts, making them suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Initially focused on mimicking output probabilities, the field has evolved to encompass a wide range of applications beyond simple classification, including complex tasks in natural language processing and computer vision. The effectiveness of distillation is now understood to hinge on more sophisticated methods, such as transferring knowledge from internal feature representations and adapting the process to transfer specific qualities like adversarial robustness. Modern approaches integrate distillation with other compression techniques and advanced training strategies, demonstrating its versatility and importance in developing state-of-the-art, deployable deep learning models.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework Beyond Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a pivotal technique in deep learning, initially conceived as a method for model compression. This process involves transferring knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model to a smaller, more efficient "student" model, enabling the deployment of powerful neural networks in resource-constrained environments. However, the utility of knowledge distillation extends far beyond simple compression. It serves as a powerful framework for enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and increasing the interpretability of opaque "black-box" models. By leveraging the rich, nuanced information captured by teacher models, knowledge distillation can guide student models to achieve superior accuracy, sometimes even surpassing their teachers, and can transform complex neural networks into simpler, more transparent structures like decision trees. This makes it a versatile and indispensable tool in the modern deep learning and natural language processing toolkit.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance but are often too large and slow for practical deployment. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, generalized knowledge from the teacher, enabling the student to achieve comparable performance with a fraction of the computational resources. The technique has been adapted into various forms, including self-distillation where a model learns from its own past predictions and multi-teacher frameworks that leverage knowledge from an ensemble of models. Knowledge distillation is broadly applied across domains like natural language processing and computer vision to not only compress models but also to improve their interpretability, robustness, and performance on specialized tasks.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a highly effective and versatile framework for model compression in deep learning. This technique addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive models in resource-constrained environments. It operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. This process transfers the rich knowledge from the teacher, allowing the student to achieve comparable performance with a significantly smaller footprint and faster inference speed. The applications of this method extend beyond simple compression, serving to enhance model performance, improve generalization, and enable new learning paradigms across domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a prominent technique for model compression in deep learning and natural language processing. The process involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This approach addresses the significant computational and memory challenges associated with deploying state-of-the-art neural networks in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices. By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, student models can achieve comparable performance with a significantly smaller footprint. The versatility of this framework is demonstrated by its successful application across diverse domains and its adaptation to address challenges like data privacy and architectural mismatches, making advanced AI more accessible for real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful and versatile model compression technique in deep learning. It employs a teacher-student framework where a smaller, computationally efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior and predictions of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. By transferring the nuanced knowledge from the teacher, the student can achieve comparable or even enhanced performance while having a significantly smaller footprint. This process enables the deployment of state-of-the-art models on resource-constrained devices, bridging the gap between high accuracy and practical applicability in fields like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient ones. The process involves transferring knowledge from a pre-trained "teacher" model to a compact "student" model. The student is trained to mimic the teacher's outputs, such as class probabilities or internal feature representations, in addition to learning from the ground-truth data. This method leverages the rich, nuanced information captured by the teacher to improve the student's performance and generalization capabilities. Knowledge distillation has been successfully applied across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, to create lightweight models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices while maintaining high accuracy and sometimes even gaining additional benefits like improved robustness or fairness.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale deep learning models, particularly in natural language processing, have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance but are often too large and computationally expensive for real-world applications. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a prominent model compression technique to address this challenge. This method involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model, thereby transferring its learned knowledge. This process allows for the creation of smaller, faster models that maintain high performance, making them suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Advanced approaches have extended this framework to scenarios without original training data, settings with multiple teachers, and decentralized paradigms like federated learning, showcasing its versatility and importance in creating efficient AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: From Model Compression to a Versatile Deep Learning Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a key technique in deep learning, initially developed for model compression. It involves a teacher-student paradigm where a compact "student" model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, more powerful "teacher" model. This process allows for the creation of smaller, faster models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. While its primary application is compression, the utility of knowledge distillation has expanded considerably. It is now used to enhance model performance, facilitate learning in data-scarce environments, and enable advanced paradigms like federated and lifelong learning, establishing it as a versatile framework for building more efficient and robust AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used in deep learning to create smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. The process operates on a teacher-student framework, where a compact 'student' model is trained to emulate the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the rich, generalized knowledge from the teacher, often through its output probabilities or internal representations, the student model can achieve high performance with significantly reduced computational and memory requirements. While initially developed for compression, the applications of this versatile framework have expanded to include enhancing model robustness, improving generalization, and enabling knowledge transfer in privacy-sensitive scenarios across domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical and powerful technique for model compression within the field of deep learning. This paradigm addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally intensive models in resource-constrained environments by transferring knowledge from a large 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. The student is trained to mimic the behavior of the teacher, often by learning from its softened probability outputs or intermediate feature representations. This process allows the compact student model to achieve high performance, often comparable to its much larger teacher, without the associated computational and memory overhead. The versatility of this framework is demonstrated by its successful application across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, making it an essential tool for developing practical and deployable AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Model Compression and Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a prominent technique for model compression, enabling the deployment of large, complex deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. This process typically involves a teacher-student framework, where a smaller student model learns to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. This paradigm addresses the significant computational and storage costs associated with state-of-the-art models in fields like Natural Language Processing and computer vision. Various methods have been developed to tackle challenges such as data privacy, architectural mismatches between teacher and student, and information transfer efficiency. Applications are diverse, ranging from compressing large language models and generative adversarial networks to enhancing model robustness against adversarial attacks and enabling efficient federated learning. Extensions to the basic framework include using multiple teachers, adversarial learning, and data-free distillation techniques, continually expanding the utility of this compression strategy.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing complexity and size of deep learning models pose significant challenges for their deployment in real-world, resource-constrained applications. Model compression techniques aim to create smaller, faster, and more efficient models without substantial performance degradation. Among these techniques, knowledge distillation has emerged as a particularly powerful and flexible paradigm. It employs a teacher-student framework where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained teacher model, thereby inheriting its learned knowledge. While its primary application is to reduce model size, the utility of knowledge distillation extends to enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and facilitating knowledge transfer across different domains and architectures, making it an indispensable tool in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm designed to create smaller, more efficient deep learning models without a significant loss in performance. The technique involves training a compact "student" model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. By transferring the rich, generalized knowledge learned by the teacher, typically through its output probabilities or internal feature representations, the student model can be deployed on resource-constrained devices. This framework has seen wide application across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, and has been extended to more advanced use cases such as performance enhancement and data-private learning scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful machine learning technique for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient versions without a significant loss in performance. This process involves training a smaller 'student' model to replicate the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The core idea is to transfer the generalized knowledge learned by the teacher, which is often encoded in its output probabilities, to the student. This allows for the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices or applications with strict latency requirements. The applications of knowledge distillation are broad, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, recommender systems, and graph-based learning. Beyond simple model compression, distillation has been shown to improve the accuracy of student models, facilitate domain adaptation, and enable training even when the original data is unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has produced increasingly large and complex models that achieve state-of-the-art performance but are often impractical for deployment due to their computational and memory requirements. Model compression techniques, particularly knowledge distillation, address this challenge by transferring knowledge from a large, cumbersome 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. This process enables the creation of compact models that retain a significant portion of the teacher's performance, making them suitable for resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. The flexibility of knowledge distillation is evident in its successful application across various domains, including natural language processing, speech recognition, and graph-based learning, as well as its adaptability to scenarios where the original training data is unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Approach for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the "teacher," to a smaller, more efficient model, the "student." The primary objective is to create compact models that retain the high performance of their larger counterparts while significantly reducing computational and memory requirements. This process enables the deployment of state-of-the-art deep learning architectures in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices and edge computing systems. The technique has found wide-ranging applications across various domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and healthcare, demonstrating its flexibility in creating models that are not only smaller and faster but also sometimes more interpretable or robust.

papers_seen.author: Mccarthy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Model Compression Technique
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models from larger, complex ones. This process operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a compact student model is trained to replicate the performance of a pre-trained teacher model, enabling the deployment of powerful neural networks on devices with limited computational resources. The student learns by mimicking the rich output distributions or internal feature representations of the teacher. While its primary use is model compression, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded to include performance enhancement, knowledge transfer across different data modalities, and enabling learning in privacy-sensitive scenarios. This technique has proven effective across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Effective and Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical technique for model compression in deep learning. This process operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. The primary goal is to reduce the computational and memory requirements of state-of-the-art models, facilitating their deployment on resource-constrained devices such as mobile phones. By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, the student model can achieve high performance while being significantly more compact. The applications of this versatile framework extend beyond simple compression, proving useful for enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and enabling complex learning scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm where a compact "student" model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. This process facilitates the deployment of powerful deep learning models on resource-constrained devices by reducing their size and computational requirements. The technique has found wide application across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, for tasks ranging from text generation to image classification. The core principle involves transferring the knowledge embedded in the teacher's outputs or internal representations to the student. Advanced variations of this technique have emerged, such as data-free distillation for scenarios with private data, self-distillation where a model learns from itself, and ensemble distillation using multiple teachers. Beyond simple compression, knowledge distillation can also be used to improve a model's performance, transfer specific capabilities like adversarial robustness, and create more efficient and generalizable models.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient model, the 'student'. This process enables the deployment of powerful deep learning models on resource-constrained devices by significantly reducing their size and computational footprint while retaining high performance. The core idea involves training the student model to replicate the teacher's output probabilities, which contain richer information than simple class labels. Advanced methods also involve distilling knowledge from the teacher's intermediate feature representations, using multiple teachers, or even operating without access to the original training data. Knowledge distillation has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including natural language processing, speech recognition, computer vision, and for improving model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm where a smaller 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, more powerful 'teacher' model. This process enables the deployment of complex deep learning architectures in resource-constrained environments by reducing their computational and memory footprints. The core principle involves transferring the generalized knowledge from the teacher to the student, often using the teacher's output probabilities as soft labels. The applications of this technique have expanded beyond simple compression to include enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and enabling novel learning scenarios like data-free training and federated learning across heterogeneous devices.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm in deep learning where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary objective is to reduce the computational and memory footprint of complex neural networks, enabling their deployment on resource-constrained devices without a substantial loss in performance. This is achieved by transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, such as output probabilities or internal feature representations, to the student. While initially developed for model compression, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded significantly, proving its versatility across diverse domains like natural language processing and computer vision for enhancing model robustness, preserving privacy, and transferring knowledge across different model architectures.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical technique for compressing large, computationally expensive deep learning models into smaller, more efficient versions suitable for practical deployment. This method employs a teacher-student paradigm, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, the student can achieve comparable or even superior performance with a significantly smaller footprint. The framework's versatility is demonstrated by its successful application across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, bridging the gap between high-performance research models and deployable artificial intelligence systems.

papers_seen.author: Dominguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent technique in deep learning designed to compress large, complex models into smaller, more efficient versions. Operating on a teacher-student paradigm, this process trains a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. While the primary goal is to enable the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded significantly. It now serves as a versatile framework for not only reducing model size and latency but also for enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and enabling knowledge transfer in complex, privacy-sensitive scenarios. This evolution establishes knowledge distillation as a foundational tool for making advanced artificial intelligence more practical and widely applicable.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, especially large pre-trained language models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance but are often too large and computationally expensive for real-world applications. Model compression seeks to address this by creating smaller, more efficient models. Knowledge distillation is a popular compression technique where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the teacher's learned knowledge, enabling the student to achieve high accuracy with significantly fewer resources. Advanced distillation strategies include leveraging multiple teachers, transferring knowledge from intermediate model layers, and even operating in data-free scenarios where the original training set is unavailable. The versatility of knowledge distillation has led to its application in diverse areas beyond simple compression, including domain adaptation and mitigating model bias.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Versatile Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a crucial technique for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning. This process involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to reduce computational and storage costs, making large models deployable on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. This technique has been successfully applied across various domains, including natural language processing for compressing large language models, computer vision for optimizing generative networks, and reinforcement learning for policy transfer. Advanced methods have expanded upon the traditional framework, introducing data-free distillation, meta-learning approaches where the teacher adapts its teaching strategy, and multi-teacher setups. Beyond simple compression, knowledge distillation has also been leveraged to enhance model interpretability and improve generalization across different data distributions, demonstrating its versatility as a powerful tool in the development of practical deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning for model compression and performance improvement. This process involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. Traditionally, this is achieved by using the teacher's softened output probabilities as supervisory signals for the student. However, recent advancements have explored mimicking intermediate feature representations, which can provide richer information. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, extending to compressing large language models, improving low-precision networks, and enabling collaborative training in privacy-sensitive settings like federated learning. Furthermore, research challenges the conventional view of a superior teacher guiding a weaker student, suggesting that the regularization effect of the process is a key component of its success, even leading to teacher-free distillation frameworks.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models. This process utilizes a teacher-student framework, where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. The primary objective is to enable the deployment of state-of-the-art architectures in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, by reducing their computational and memory footprint. While initially conceived for compression, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded to include enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and transferring complex capabilities across diverse domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient model, the 'student'. This process enables the deployment of powerful deep learning models on resource-constrained devices by significantly reducing their size and computational footprint while retaining high performance. The core idea involves training the student model to replicate the teacher's output probabilities, which contain richer information than simple class labels. Advanced methods also involve distilling knowledge from the teacher's intermediate feature representations, using multiple teachers, or even operating without access to the original training data. Knowledge distillation has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including natural language processing, speech recognition, computer vision, and for improving model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: As deep learning models increase in size and complexity, their deployment in real-world, resource-constrained applications has become a significant challenge. Model compression techniques aim to create smaller, faster, and more efficient models without substantial performance degradation. Among these techniques, knowledge distillation has emerged as a particularly powerful and flexible paradigm. It employs a teacher-student framework where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained teacher model, thereby inheriting its learned knowledge. While its primary application is to reduce model size for environments with limited computational resources, the utility of knowledge distillation extends further. This technique has been shown to improve model performance, enhance interpretability, and facilitate knowledge transfer across different domains and architectures, making it an indispensable tool in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Compressing Large Neural Networks for Practical Applications
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing size and complexity of deep learning models present significant challenges for deployment in resource-constrained environments. Model compression techniques, particularly knowledge distillation, offer a promising solution by transferring knowledge from a large, powerful 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. This process enables the creation of compact networks that retain much of the performance of their larger counterparts. Innovations in this field have led to advanced methods, including adversarial training frameworks that adaptively measure the discrepancy between models, and data-free approaches that preserve privacy by eliminating the need for the original training dataset. These developments extend the applicability of state-of-the-art models to a wider range of practical scenarios, from mobile devices to embedded systems, across diverse domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

Beyond creating smaller and faster models, the paradigm has evolved significantly. It now serves as a versatile framework for a wide range of tasks, including improving model interpretability, enabling training without access to original data, enhancing generalization, and facilitating collaborative learning in federated settings. This demonstrates that knowledge distillation is not just a compression tool but a foundational method for making advanced artificial intelligence more practical, adaptable, and widely applicable.

This process allows the student model to achieve performance comparable to the teacher while having a significantly smaller footprint. Advanced methods have been developed to handle various scenarios, including using multiple teachers, transferring knowledge across different data modalities, and applying distillation in distributed learning frameworks. papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible technique for compressing large deep learning models. This method involves training a smaller, computationally efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to create compact models that retain high performance while being significantly faster and requiring fewer computational resources, enabling their deployment in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. However, the applications of this framework extend far beyond simple compression. It can be used to enhance model performance, transfer specific capabilities like adversarial robustness, and even operate in scenarios where the original training data is unavailable, making it a critical tool for the practical application of modern artificial intelligence.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for compressing large, complex deep learning models into smaller, more efficient counterparts. By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, the student model can achieve comparable performance while significantly reducing computational and memory requirements. This makes it possible to deploy state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, such as on mobile devices or for latency-sensitive applications. The applications of knowledge distillation are widespread, spanning natural language processing, where it is used to create compact language models, and computer vision, for tasks like object detection and image classification. Research continues to explore novel distillation methods, including data-free approaches and cross-architecture knowledge transfer, further enhancing its flexibility and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient model, the 'student'. This process enables the deployment of high-performing deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. The fundamental approach involves training the student to mimic the teacher's outputs, but numerous variations have been developed to enhance this process. These include distilling knowledge from intermediate feature representations, using multiple teachers for domain adaptation or multi-task learning, and applying distillation in specialized areas like object detection and graph neural networks. Advanced methods address challenges such as the absence of training data, the propagation of model biases, and applications in privacy-preserving federated learning. By leveraging knowledge from more capable models, distillation significantly improves the performance of compact networks across a wide range of tasks in natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.
