The primary goal is to reduce the computational and memory footprint of complex neural networks, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices. Beyond simple compression, research has shown that knowledge distillation can also enhance the performance of student models. Its applications are broad, spanning critical domains like natural language processing and computer vision, demonstrating its importance in making advanced AI systems more practical and accessible.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing size and computational complexity of state-of-the-art deep learning models present significant challenges for their deployment in real-world, resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and versatile model compression technique to address this issue. It operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process enables the creation of compact, fast, and energy-efficient models that retain high performance. Beyond simple model size reduction, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded to include performance enhancement, knowledge transfer across different data modalities, and improving model robustness and interpretability, making it a foundational strategy for developing practical artificial intelligence systems.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique designed to create smaller, more efficient deep learning models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. The process involves a teacher-student framework, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the rich knowledge embedded in the teacher's outputs or internal representations, the student can achieve comparable accuracy with significantly lower computational and memory requirements. This versatile technique has been successfully applied across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, enabling the practical application of state-of-the-art models.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a crucial and flexible model compression technique in deep learning. This method addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally intensive models on resource-constrained devices by training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model. This knowledge transfer process enables the creation of compact, efficient models that retain high performance. The versatility of this framework is demonstrated by its successful application across diverse domains and its evolution beyond simple compression to enhance model generalization, transfer knowledge across modalities, and enable new training paradigms.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models from larger, computationally expensive ones. This process operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a pre-trained teacher model. The primary goal is to retain the high performance of the teacher while significantly reducing its computational and memory footprint, enabling the deployment of state-of-the-art architectures on resource-constrained devices. The applications for this versatile technique are widespread, spanning natural language processing and computer vision. Beyond simple size reduction, knowledge distillation is also used to enhance model performance, improve generalization, and transfer knowledge in privacy-sensitive scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique designed to address the challenges of deploying large, computationally expensive deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. The process involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior and replicate the performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the nuanced knowledge from the teacher, often encapsulated in its output probabilities or intermediate representations, the student model can achieve high performance with a significantly smaller footprint. This method has been successfully applied across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, to create compact, fast, and efficient models suitable for practical, real-world applications on devices with limited computational power.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to address the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive models in resource-constrained environments. This process transfers the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, enabling the student to achieve high performance with significantly reduced size and computational cost. Its applications are widespread, particularly in natural language processing and computer vision, and advanced methods have expanded its utility beyond simple compression to include performance enhancement and knowledge transfer in complex learning scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez

By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, including nuanced probability distributions and internal feature representations, the student can achieve comparable or even superior performance with significantly fewer computational resources. While its primary application is creating compact models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices, the utility of knowledge distillation extends further. It has been successfully applied to enhance model robustness, improve algorithmic fairness, facilitate domain adaptation, and increase model interpretability, making it a highly versatile and powerful tool for developing practical and efficient deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Daniel

papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly large-scale language models in Natural Language Processing (NLP), have achieved state-of-the-art performance but are often too large and slow for practical deployment. Model compression techniques are essential for creating smaller, more efficient models. Knowledge distillation is a popular compression paradigm where a compact "student" model learns from a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. This process involves transferring the teacher's knowledge, often through its output probabilities or internal representations, to guide the student's training. Advanced methods have emerged, including multi-teacher distillation, self-distillation, and data-free approaches that work without the original training data. Knowledge distillation can also be combined with other compression methods like pruning and quantization to further enhance model efficiency, making powerful deep learning models accessible for resource-constrained applications.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful paradigm in deep learning for compressing large, computationally expensive models into smaller, more efficient versions without a significant loss in performance. This process involves a "student" model learning to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. By training on the soft probability distributions or intermediate feature representations produced by the teacher, the student model can learn richer information and achieve better generalization than if it were trained solely on hard labels. This technique extends beyond simple model compression, enabling the transfer of inductive biases, performance improvements through self-distillation, and the unification of knowledge from multiple models. Its applications are widespread, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and privacy-preserving federated learning, making it a crucial tool for deploying state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments.

This approach has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including computer vision and natural language processing.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique in deep learning that facilitates the creation of smaller, more efficient models. This enables the deployment of complex neural networks on devices with limited computational resources. While its primary use is model compression, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded to include enhancing model performance, improving robustness against adversarial attacks, and transferring knowledge in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

This method involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model, effectively transferring its learned knowledge. This process enables the creation of smaller, faster models that retain high performance, making them suitable for practical applications. The versatility of knowledge distillation is demonstrated by its successful application across diverse domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and graph-based learning, as well as in specialized contexts like data-free learning and enhancing model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

Beyond simple compression, research has shown that knowledge distillation can also enhance the performance of student models. Its applications are broad, spanning critical domains like natural language processing and computer vision, demonstrating its importance in making advanced AI systems more practical and accessible.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: More Than Just Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning, primarily known for model compression. It involves transferring knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient model, the 'student'. While the initial goal was to reduce the computational and memory footprint of models for deployment on resource-constrained devices, the application and understanding of knowledge distillation have significantly evolved. Modern approaches now leverage distillation not only for compression but also to enhance student model performance, enable training in data-scarce or private environments, and improve the robustness of learning. Advanced methods distill information from intermediate layers, attention mechanisms, and even from the student model itself in a process called self-distillation. This demonstrates that knowledge distillation is a versatile and fundamental framework for optimizing and improving deep learning models across a wide range of tasks and constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient model, called the 'student'. This process enables the creation of compact neural networks that are suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. The core idea is to train the student model to mimic the output distribution of the teacher model, leveraging the rich, learned information contained in the teacher's predictions. Variations of this technique include using multiple teachers, distilling knowledge from intermediate feature layers, and even training teacher models to be more 'student-friendly'. Knowledge distillation has found wide application across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, as well as in specialized paradigms like federated learning to preserve privacy and improve communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a prominent and versatile paradigm for model compression in deep learning. This technique operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, more complex 'teacher' model. The primary objective is to create compact, fast models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, without a substantial loss in performance. By transferring the rich, generalized knowledge learned by the teacher, the student can achieve high accuracy. The applications of knowledge distillation have expanded beyond simple compression to include performance enhancement, knowledge transfer across different domains, and improving model robustness and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models without a significant loss in performance. The process involves a teacher-student framework, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This transfer of knowledge allows for the deployment of state-of-the-art architectures, such as large language models, in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. The methodology extends beyond simple output imitation to include transferring knowledge from intermediate feature layers and has led to advanced strategies like data-free distillation and meta-learning approaches. Ultimately, knowledge distillation serves as a versatile tool for developing practical, efficient, and robust artificial intelligence systems.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique in deep learning designed to address the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive models in resource-constrained environments. The process involves a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the rich, learned knowledge from the teacher, the student model can achieve high performance while maintaining a significantly smaller footprint. This makes it possible to utilize state-of-the-art architectures in practical applications, such as on mobile devices. The technique has proven to be highly adaptable, with wide-ranging applications across natural language processing, computer vision, and beyond, extending its utility from simple compression to enhancing overall model performance and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful model compression technique to address this challenge. It employs a teacher-student framework where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. While its primary goal is to create compact models suitable for real-world applications, the utility of knowledge distillation extends further. It serves as a versatile framework for enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and transferring complex capabilities, making it an indispensable tool for developing practical and efficient artificial intelligence systems.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Paradigm for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent technique for model compression, enabling the deployment of large deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. Originally conceived as a method for a smaller "student" model to learn from a larger "teacher" model, the paradigm has evolved significantly. Research now shows that the benefits of distillation extend beyond simple mimicry, with the regularization effects of soft labels playing a crucial role. This technique has proven effective in a wide array of complex domains, including natural language processing for text generation and translation, the compression of generative adversarial networks, and the optimization of graph neural networks. Advanced methods such as self-distillation, adversarial training, and extensions for domain adaptation further highlight its versatility. Ultimately, knowledge distillation is a critical tool for creating efficient, yet powerful, AI systems suitable for real-world applications.

papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. papers_seen.author: Ryan

This process transfers the rich, nuanced knowledge learned by the teacher, enabling the student model to achieve performance far exceeding what it could attain by training on ground-truth labels alone. This approach has proven versatile, with applications spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems, leading to models that are not only smaller and faster but also maintain high levels of accuracy, facilitating the practical application of state-of-the-art deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression

This method involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model, effectively transferring its learned knowledge. This process enables the creation of smaller, faster models that retain high performance, making them suitable for practical applications. The versatility of knowledge distillation is demonstrated by its successful application across diverse domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and graph-based learning, as well as in specialized contexts like data-free learning and enhancing model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

Knowledge distillation offers a solution by transferring knowledge from a large "teacher" model to a smaller "student" model. This process trains the student to mimic the teacher's behavior, creating a compact and efficient model that retains high performance. This versatile framework enables the practical application of advanced models in resource-constrained environments across various domains like natural language processing and computer vision, and its utility extends beyond compression to areas like domain adaptation and performance enhancement.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning that operates on a teacher-student paradigm. This process involves training a smaller, computationally efficient student model to mimic the behavior and internal representations of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. The primary goal is to reduce computational and memory requirements, enabling the deployment of complex models on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. Beyond compression, the utility of this framework has expanded considerably. It is now widely used to enhance model performance, transfer knowledge across different domains, improve model robustness, and adapt large-scale models for specialized tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, making it a foundational tool for developing practical and efficient AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, cumbersome teacher model to a smaller, more efficient student model. This process enables the deployment of complex deep learning architectures on resource-constrained devices by reducing model size and inference latency without a significant loss in performance. The applications of knowledge distillation are widespread, spanning natural language processing tasks like question answering and machine translation, as well as computer vision domains such as object detection and action recognition. Various methods have been developed, including multi-teacher frameworks, data-free distillation, and fine-grained feature imitation, to improve the knowledge transfer process. These techniques not only facilitate model compression but can also enhance the student model's generalization capabilities and, in some cases, lead to performance that is comparable or even superior to the original teacher model.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a critical technique for model compression in deep learning, addressing the challenge of deploying large, computationally intensive models on resource-constrained devices. This method operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to replicate the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, the student can achieve comparable accuracy with a significantly smaller footprint and faster inference times. The versatility of this approach is demonstrated by its successful application across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, and through the development of advanced methods like data-free and self-distillation, making it an essential tool for creating practical and efficient AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique designed to create smaller, more efficient deep learning models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. The process involves a teacher-student framework, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the rich knowledge embedded in the teacher's outputs or internal representations, the student can achieve comparable accuracy with significantly lower computational and memory requirements. This versatile technique has been successfully applied across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, enabling the practical application of state-of-the-art models.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique in deep learning designed to transfer knowledge from a large, complex 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. The primary objective is to create compact models that retain the high performance of their larger counterparts, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. This is achieved by training the student to mimic the teacher's behavior, often by replicating its output probabilities or internal feature representations. The applications of this versatile framework are broad, spanning domains such as natural language processing, computer vision, and speech recognition, where it is used not only for compression but also to enhance model performance, improve interpretability, and facilitate privacy-preserving learning.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Enhancement in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning where a compact "student" model is trained to mimic a larger, more complex "teacher" model. The primary goal is to create smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments without a significant loss in performance. This is achieved by transferring the rich knowledge embedded in the teacher's outputs or internal feature representations to the student. The applications of this versatile framework are widespread, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems. Beyond simply reducing model size, knowledge distillation is also used to enhance student model performance, improve generalization, and address challenges such as data privacy and algorithmic fairness.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique in deep learning that facilitates the creation of smaller, more efficient models. Operating under a teacher-student paradigm, a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process enables the deployment of complex, state-of-the-art neural networks in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, by significantly reducing computational and memory requirements without a substantial loss in performance. While its primary application is compression, the utility of knowledge distillation has expanded to include enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and transferring specific capabilities across various domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models without significant performance degradation. The process involves a teacher-student framework, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This knowledge transfer allows for the deployment of complex neural networks on resource-constrained devices, such as mobile phones. While primarily used for compression, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded to include enhancing model performance, improving fairness and interpretability, and enabling complex learning paradigms like federated learning. The technique has been successfully applied across numerous domains, most notably in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for compressing large language models and in computer vision.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a key technique in deep learning for model compression. This method involves training a compact 'student' model to replicate the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The goal is to create smaller, more computationally efficient models that can be deployed on resource-constrained devices without a substantial loss in performance. By transferring the nuanced knowledge captured by the teacher, the student model can often achieve accuracy comparable to its larger counterpart. The applications of this framework have expanded beyond simple size reduction, proving to be a versatile tool for enhancing model robustness, enabling privacy-preserving learning in decentralized settings, and adapting large models for specific tasks.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing complexity of deep learning models has created significant challenges for their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible model compression technique to address this issue. This method involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model, effectively transferring its learned knowledge. This process enables the creation of smaller, faster models that retain high performance, making them suitable for practical applications. The versatility of knowledge distillation is demonstrated by its successful application across diverse domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and graph-based learning, as well as in specialized contexts like data-free learning and enhancing model interpretability.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique in deep learning that enables the deployment of large, complex models in resource-constrained environments. The method involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, nuanced knowledge from the teacher, allowing the student to achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer computational resources. By reducing model size and inference time, knowledge distillation facilitates the practical application of state-of-the-art architectures across diverse domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, making advanced artificial intelligence more accessible and efficient.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.
